description: Believing append always copies, so the returned slice never shares backing storage with the original and writes through one cannot be seen through the other.
Believing a slice is passed by reference, so append inside a function changes the caller's length, rather than the header being copied by value.
Believing s[1:3] copies elements into a new array instead of creating a view over the same backing array.
Believing len and cap are the same thing, so make([]int, 5) and make([]int, 0, 5) are interchangeable.
Believing a nil slice must be initialised before use, rather than being a valid empty slice that supports len, range and append.
Believing you can assign into a nil map the way you can append to a nil slice, instead of it panicking without make.
Believing reading an absent map key panics or returns nil, rather than yielding the value type's zero value.
Believing map iteration follows insertion order or sorted key order, rather than being deliberately randomised.
Believing you can assign to a field of a struct value stored in a map (m[k].f = v) without the map holding a pointer.
Believing arrays and slices are the same, so [3]int and []int are interchangeable and arrays are passed by reference.
Believing the range value variable aliases the element, so mutating it or taking its address modifies the collection.
Believing the ranged expression and its length are re-evaluated each iteration, so appending inside the loop extends it.
Assuming (or in modern Go, still fearing) that goroutines and closures capture one shared loop variable, misjudging per-iteration scoping rules.
Believing defer runs at the end of the enclosing block or loop iteration rather than when the surrounding function returns.
Believing deferred call arguments and the receiver are evaluated when the deferred call runs, not at the point of the defer statement.
Believing a deferred function cannot alter the returned value, overlooking that it can modify named result parameters after return.
Believing go f() waits for f to finish, or that main waits for running goroutines before exiting.
Believing a send on an unbuffered channel returns immediately and buffers one value, rather than blocking until a receiver is ready.
Believing receives on a closed channel block or panic, rather than returning the zero value immediately with ok == false.
Believing every channel must be closed to avoid leaks, or that the receiver may close a channel, rather than close signalling no more sends.
Believing operations on a nil channel panic or succeed, instead of blocking forever and thus disabling a select case.
Believing select evaluates cases top to bottom and picks the first listed ready case, rather than choosing uniformly at random among ready cases.
Believing wg.Add may be called inside the spawned goroutine, or that passing a WaitGroup by value still coordinates correctly.
Believing a struct containing a sync.Mutex can be copied or passed by value and still provide mutual exclusion.
Believing that using channels or goroutines anywhere makes all shared-variable access safe, so no mutex or atomic is ever needed.
Believing an interface holding a typed nil pointer compares equal to nil, so err != nil is false when a nil *MyError is returned.
Believing a type must explicitly declare that it implements an interface, rather than satisfaction being structural and implicit.
Believing a value of type T satisfies an interface whose methods have pointer receivers, ignoring addressability and method-set rules.
Believing a method with a value receiver can mutate the original struct, instead of operating on a copy.
Believing struct embedding is subclassing with virtual dispatch, so the outer type's method overrides calls made from the embedded type's methods.
Believing s[i] yields a one-character string or a rune, rather than a byte, and that len(s) counts characters rather than bytes.
Believing a string can be modified in place via s[i] = 'x', rather than being immutable and requiring a []byte or []rune conversion.
Believing repeated s += x in a loop mutates in place at no cost, rather than allocating a new string each time where a Builder is preferable.
Believing Go implicitly converts between numeric types, so int and int64 or int and float64 can be mixed in an expression without a conversion.
Believing 3/2 produces 1.5, rather than integer division truncating toward zero when both operands are integers.
Confusing T(x) conversion with x.(T) type assertion, expecting one to do the other's runtime interface check.
Believing panic/recover is Go's normal error mechanism and that a panic in one goroutine can be recovered by another or by the caller's recover.
Believing wrapped errors can be matched with == or by comparing message strings, rather than with errors.Is and errors.As.
Believing visibility is controlled by keywords or file layout rather than identifier capitalisation, and that unexported fields marshal to JSON.
Believing := always assigns to the existing outer variable, missing that in a new scope it declares and shadows a fresh variable.
